title: Concentration and the Nernst equation

concepts.label: non-standard conditions
concepts.definition: Any state of a cell in which the ion concentrations are not all 1 mol/L (or the temperature is not 25 °C), so the voltage differs from E°cell.

concepts.label: more reactant ion → more push
concepts.definition: Le Chatelier intuition for a cell: raising the concentration of an ion the reaction consumes raises the voltage, and piling up an ion it produces lowers it.

concepts.label: reaction quotient Q
concepts.definition: Product ion concentrations divided by reactant ion concentrations, each raised to its coefficient, with pure solids left out; Q = 1 at standard conditions and it grows as a cell discharges (Daniell cell: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]).

concepts.label: 59 mV per decade
concepts.definition: At 25 °C every tenfold increase in Q lowers the cell voltage by 59.2 mV divided by n, the number of electrons transferred (29.6 mV for the Daniell cell).

concepts.label: Nernst equation
concepts.definition: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, which at 25 °C is E° − (0.0592 V/n) log₁₀ Q; it gives the voltage of a cell or the potential of a single electrode at any concentrations.

concepts.label: concentration cell
concepts.definition: A cell with the same metal and ion in both half-cells but different concentrations: E° = 0, the voltage is (59.2 mV/n) per tenfold concentration difference, and it runs until the concentrations are equal.

concepts.label: dead cell = equilibrium
concepts.definition: A cell reads 0 V when forward and reverse reactions happen equally often so nothing changes any more (equilibrium); this is where the Q term of the Nernst equation exactly cancels E°, and ΔG = 0.

concepts.label: equilibrium constant K from E°
concepts.definition: K is the value of Q at equilibrium; setting E = 0 in the Nernst equation gives log₁₀ K = nE°/0.0592 V at 25 °C (Daniell cell: K ≈ 10³⁷).

namedOnly: Le Chatelier's principle (named as the pattern behind 'more reactant → more push')
activity (effective concentration; the course uses plain mol/L)
gas constant R and thermal voltage RT/F ≈ 25.7 mV (explained in one paragraph, not a tracked concept)
pH / pH electrode (one-line application: about 59 mV per tenfold change in [H⁺])
discharge curve shape (plateau then cliff; internal-resistance losses deferred to Real batteries)
summary: Running example: the Daniell cell (Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, E° = 1.10 V, n = 2) at changing ion concentrations, with Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]; side examples are a Zn–Ag cell (squared term in Q), a Cu/Cu²⁺ concentration cell and a Sn/Pb²⁺ pair with K ≈ 2. The capstone is a Daniell discharge simulator: constant current converts Cu²⁺ to Zn²⁺ via Faraday's constant, voltage follows Nernst, and the cell dies at Q = K ≈ 10³⁷ (revivable by adding CuSO₄). Hooks for later lessons: 'voltage = E° minus 59.2 mV/n per decade of Q', 'plateau then cliff' discharge shape, 'voltage is a poor fuel gauge', 'dead = equilibrium (ΔG = 0)', the half-cell form of Nernst (electrode levels slide on the potential ladder), and the explicit note that current-dependent losses are not modelled here.

sources.title: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, §17.4 Potential, Free Energy, and Equilibrium
